title: Panthalassa, floating data centers, and the power of the ocean
html:
Some 250 million years ago, much of the Earth was covered by a superocean known as Panthalassa.

Surrounding the supercontinent Pangea during the Paleozoic–Mesozoic transition, its waters coated some 70 percent of the planet’s surface,

The original Panthalassa is long gone (its direct continuation is today’s Pacific Ocean), but the name lives on thanks to a startup that hopes to use energy from waves to power data centers.

Having raised millions of dollars from some of the biggest names in tech, Panthalassa is hoping to put its first craft out at sea in 2027.

An energy play

Panthalassa, the company, was founded by Garth Sheldon-Coulson in 2017. While this was long before ChatGPT and Claude became main characters in our lives, Sheldon-Coulson, who at the time worked for investment manager Bridgewater Associates, says it was already clear that the tide of compute was rising.

“It was obvious back then that compute energy demand growth was going to be exponential,” he says. “While I was at Bridgewater, I saw some of the early work going on with LLMs (large language models), and if you traced the curves forward, it was clear that the energy demands of compute would intersect with total grid capacity somewhere around 2030.

“When compute energy demand outstrips infrastructure, you’ve got a problem, because you can scale compute exponentially, but you can’t do that with energy. We said to ourselves: the world needs another energy source, and it needs to be scalable and benign ecologically, so that it’s harmonious with the natural environment and doesn’t conflict with areas like agriculture.”

Together with co-founder Brian Moffat, Sheldon-Coulson assessed the available options for generating the terawatts of required power, and alighted upon wave energy as the best option.

“The middle of the ocean, far from the shore, is a power-dense resource,” he says. “The winds are blowing all the time, and creating waves, and we realized we could take advantage of these attributes and do it really cheaply. You also get really good cooling, because the temperature is a lot lower out at sea, so the whole picture came together in our minds.”

Inside the node

The system that Panthalassa has devised to harness ocean power is installed in autonomous craft the company refers to as Nodes (“This is potentially confusing, as they can contain many compute nodes,” Sheldon-Coulson notes) that propel themselves out to sea, capture energy from the waves, and host the payload, the compute cluster, on board.

“It’s an integrated unit, which allows us to be untethered from any other infrastructure,” Sheldon-Coulson says.

The Nodes generate power in a similar manner to a hydroelectric dam; waves push water into a pressurized reservoir, which feeds an energy-generating turbine. Sheldon-Coulson says there are more than enough waves to keep the turbine turning. “You might get variable flow in, but the reservoir has a stable level, and that allows you to generate power in a constant way,” he explains.

When floating on the water, the Nodes have the look of a giant table tennis ball being batted around by waves. But looks can be deceiving, and below the surface is a tapered construction that is more reminiscent of a rocket. “We build them at the factory and put them in the water horizontally,” says Sheldon-Coulson. “Then they get towed out to sea, maybe 50-100 miles, and flipped. They immediately start generating power, and they’re self-propelled in this configuration. They don’t use propellers; the way the units are shaped causes them to move forward, and means they can bounce along their way, or hold position, without using any of the energy generated.”

The Nodes come with an autonomous system that helps them steer clear of other craft, and stops them wandering back too close to shore, though Sheldon-Coulson says his team can take control of the craft in an emergency. The CEO argues the non-tethered nature of the Nodes is a big selling point for the company: “We can steer them, cause them to go round in circles or even in figures of eight,” he says. “That means we can designate deployment regions, and have a whole fleet of them out there in that region. There’s no need to drill them into the seafloor, or use any anchors or moorings, which are some of the more challenging parts of marine engineering.”

GPUs at sea

The amount of power generated by the Nodes, and therefore the amount of compute they can contain, depends on how large they are. Sheldon-Coulson says the company can construct craft of various sizes, generating “anywhere from 200kW-800kW, but we think the economic optimum will probably be around 400kW.”

Hardware is housed in a special hardened enclosure that, according to Sheldon-Coulson, serves as a type of rack. “Everything is hermetically sealed,” he says. “It’s a fully-sealed enclosure that is liquid-cooled using a freshwater loop that exchanges water with the ocean. The compute has no idea that it’s at sea, except that it experiences this relatively slow movement, akin to being in an elevator.”

Connectivity is provided via low Earth orbit satellite, and Panthalassa believes networks such as Starlink will provide more than enough bandwidth, though it is also investigating other networking technologies.

Though the company is not disclosing full details of its business model, or whether it intends to partner with a hyperscaler or neocloud, Sheldon-Coulson suggests it will have a “vertically-integrated” offering targeted at the burgeoning AI inferencing market.

“Fundamentally we’re offering a device that’s optimized for inference and reinforcement learning,” he says. “We’re not a generic platform for all manner of data center applications, but for those applications that live within our envelope, we can offer low costs and exceptional scalability.”

Time to make a splash

While Panthalassa’s development has been a long-term project for Sheldon-Coulson and his team (some of the company’s patents were first registered in 2017), its entry into the data center market could be well-timed.

With AI putting an unprecedented strain on digital infrastructure, several data center operators are looking to put compute out at sea, either floating on the surface or underwater. DCD wrote a long-form feature on this growing section of the market in issue 62 of DCD Magazine.

Investors are also swimming in the wake of Panthalassa’s vision. Earlier this year, the firm raised $140 million in a Series B funding round led by PayPal founder Peter Thiel. Though often seen as one of tech’s bogeymen due to his long-term support of Donald Trump, and his backing of the controversial big data and surveillance firm Palantir, Thiel’s involvement adds credibility to Panthalassa’s pitch. “The future demands more compute than we can imagine,” Thiel said at the time of the investment. “Extra-terrestrial solutions are no longer science fiction. Panthalassa has opened the ocean frontier.”

The company has since taken investment from Korean cloud firm Naver in a round that valued it at $2 billion, and will be raising funds again in 2027. Its next milestone will be the launch of a commercial demonstrator fleet it is calling Ocean-3. This will be located off the Pacific Northwest coast of the US, near Panthalassa’s headquarters in Portland, and the company hopes it will help show the scalability of its platform. “That will help us dial in our manufacturing process, which is intended to help us build them extremely quickly,” Sheldon-Coulson says. “Once we have the fleet operating and doing inference, we can start building our gigafactories.”

Indeed, Sheldon-Coulson says his firm will be manufacturing its own Nodes, and has a plan to build factories capable of churning out “gigawatts” of hardware each year. While it seems unlikely the Nodes will ever cover as much of the Earth’s surface as the original Panthalassa, the company will be hoping their impact amounts to more than a drop in the ocean.
summary: Peter Thiel-backed startup has big plans to put compute at sea
